The radiation didn't stay put, either. Thirty-eight years later, a big part of what I take from it is how much damage the secrecy did, on top of the accident itself. Thinking of the firefighters, the cleanup workers, and the families who lost their homes and their health.

By evening the fortress had fallen, and its governor had been killed. Taking it showed that ordinary Parisians could challenge royal power directly, and within weeks the old system of noble privileges began to come apart. The building was demolished stone by stone, and some of those stones were carved into little Bastille models and sent around the country as souvenirs of the revolution. A year later, the first anniversary was celebrated as a festival of national unity, and in 1880 France made July 14 its national holiday.

TOPIC:
Sometimes you can smell rain before the rain reaches you. Write a short post explaining where that smell comes from and how it can arrive before the first drops.
raw_text: Stood on the porch last night and caught that rain smell a good ten minutes before a single drop hit, so of course I went down a rabbit hole. Part of it is ozone. Lightning splits oxygen in the air, and the storm's downdrafts push that sharp, almost chlorine-like scent out ahead of the clouds. The earthy part is called petrichor, and a lot of it comes from geosmin, a compound made by bacteria living in the soil. Our noses are absurdly sensitive to it, way more than sharks are to blood, apparently. When the first drops land on dry ground somewhere upwind, they kick up tiny bubbles that carry those scents into the air, and the wind brings them to you before the rain itself shows up. Plants add to it too, since they let oils build up in the dirt during dry spells. So that smell is basically the storm's advance notice. 🌧️

TOPIC:
Why can a metal bench feel much colder than a wooden bench even when both have been outside at exactly the same temperature? Explain it in a way that would work in a short science post.
raw_text: Sat down on a metal bench at the bus stop this morning and nearly jumped back up. The wooden bench right next to it felt fine, even though both had been sitting out in the same 2°C air all night, so they were the exact same temperature. The difference is how fast each material pulls heat out of you. Metal is a great conductor, so the second you touch it, it drags warmth away from your skin and spreads it through the whole bench. Wood is a poor conductor, so only a thin layer right under you warms up, and then it pretty much stops taking your heat. Your skin doesn't actually sense temperature directly. It senses how quickly you're losing heat, and the metal was just stealing it faster. Same reason a tile bathroom floor feels colder on bare feet than the bath mat sitting on it.

raw_text: Sat on the porch during last night's storm and my nephew asked why the flash always comes before the boom if they're the same thing. Turns out the answer is just that light is absurdly fast and sound isn't. The flash reaches you basically the instant it happens, but the thunder crawls along at about 340 meters per second, so it falls further behind the farther away the strike is. That means the gap tells you how far off the lightning was: count the seconds, then divide by 3 for kilometers or by 5 for miles. We counted 9 seconds on one, so roughly 3 km away. Air temperature changes the speed of sound a little (it's slightly faster in warm air), but not enough to throw off a porch estimate. And if the gap is under about 30 seconds, it's time to head inside, which is exactly what we did.

TOPIC:
People often say the Moon has a 'dark side.' Write a short post explaining what is misleading about that phrase and why we keep seeing nearly the same lunar face from Earth.
raw_text: Small astronomy pet peeve: the "dark side of the Moon" isn't actually dark. It gets just as much sunlight as the side facing us. During a new moon, when we can barely see the Moon at all, the far side is the half in full daylight. The better name is the "far side," because the only thing it lacks is a view of Earth. We always see roughly the same face because the Moon spins exactly once for every trip it makes around us, about 27 days each, so it keeps the same side pointed our way. That's called tidal locking: billions of years of Earth's gravity tugging on the Moon slowed its spin until the two matched up. Thanks to a slight wobble, we actually get to see about 59% of the surface over time, not just half. Pink Floyd can keep the album title, though.

TOPIC:
Why does ice float instead of sinking in liquid water? Explain the unusual property behind it and why it matters beyond a glass of iced water.
raw_text: My kid asked me last night why the ice cubes in her juice don't sink, and I realized I'd never actually thought about it. Almost every substance gets denser when it freezes, so solid chunks of it sink in the liquid version. Water does the opposite. When it freezes, the molecules lock into a hexagonal pattern held together by hydrogen bonds, and that pattern has a lot of empty space in it, so ice ends up about 9% less dense than liquid water. That's also why a forgotten soda can explodes in the freezer and why pipes burst in January. The bigger deal is lakes and ponds. Because ice floats, they freeze from the top down, and that top layer acts like a lid that keeps the water underneath from freezing solid, so fish and everything else down there can make it through winter. If ice sank, a lot of the planet's fresh water would probably be packed with ice from the bottom up, and life on Earth might look very different. Not bad for a question asked over apple juice.

When you work muscles in a way they're not used to, especially the "lowering" part of a movement like walking downhill or slowly lowering into a squat, you cause tiny bits of damage in the muscle fibers. Your body responds with inflammation and repair, and the nerves in the area get more sensitive, which is why it peaks a day or two later instead of right away. The good news is it's a normal part of adapting, and the next time you do the same workout it usually hurts a lot less. So if your legs are screaming at you today, it's not leftover acid, just your muscles rebuilding. 🦵😩

raw_text: Had a friend ask me this week why her doctor "wouldn't just give her antibiotics" for a cold, so here's the short version. Antibiotics work by attacking parts that bacteria have and our own cells don't, like the tough outer wall bacteria build around themselves or the specific machinery they use to make proteins. Bacteria are tiny living cells that can grow and multiply on their own, so there's plenty for the drug to hit. Viruses are a different thing entirely. They're basically a bit of genetic material in a protein shell, and they can't do anything until they get inside one of your cells and use it to copy themselves. No cell wall, no bacterial machinery, nothing for an antibiotic to grab onto. That's why amoxicillin does nothing for the common cold except possibly upset your stomach. Taking antibiotics you don't need also gives the bacteria already living in you a chance to become resistant, which is how we end up with infections that are hard to treat later. So yes, it's annoying, but rest, fluids, and time really are the treatment for most colds. If you're getting worse after a week or so, though, go back, because sometimes a bacterial infection does show up on top of the cold.

raw_text: Back from Tokyo and I've been wide awake at 3 a.m. every night this week, so I finally looked up what jet lag actually is. It turns out it's not just being tired from a long flight. There's a small cluster of cells in your brain that keeps a roughly 24-hour schedule, and it tells your body when to release melatonin, when to drop your temperature for sleep, even when to get hungry. When you fly across seven or eight time zones, that clock is still running on home time, so your body is gearing up for the afternoon while the hotel room is dark. The clock does reset, mostly through daylight hitting your eyes, but it only shifts about an hour or so per day, which is why it takes most of a week to feel normal. Apparently flying east is usually worse than flying west, because pushing your bedtime earlier is harder for the body than staying up later. So if you're about to travel, get outside in the morning sun once you land, and don't blame yourself if you're staring at the ceiling at 4 a.m.

QR codes can remain readable even when part of the pattern is scratched or covered. Explain in a short post how that is possible without diving into mathematical details.
raw_text: Noticed something today: the QR code on our restaurant's table sticker is half peeled off and coffee-stained, and my phone still read it instantly. Turns out that's on purpose. When a QR code is made, it doesn't just store your link once. It also packs in extra backup information spread across the whole pattern, so if some squares are missing, the scanner can work out what they should have been from the rest. Depending on how the code was generated, it can lose somewhere between about 7% and 30% of itself and still work. That's also why companies can stick their logo right in the middle of a QR code without breaking it. The one weak spot is the three big squares in the corners, because the scanner uses those to figure out where the code is and which way it's facing. Scratch one of those off and you're probably out of luck.

raw_text: Fun fact I learned this week while trying to email a giant folder: zipping it saved me almost nothing. Turns out ZIP works by finding repetition and writing it down more efficiently. But JPEG photos and MP4 videos have already been through their own, much more aggressive compression, which even throws away detail your eyes probably won't miss. By the time ZIP gets to them, most of the repetition is gone and the data looks close to random. You can't squeeze a sponge that's already been wrung out, so the ZIP ends up maybe 1-2% smaller, and sometimes even a tiny bit bigger. So if you're trying to send vacation photos, zipping them is great for bundling everything into one file, just don't expect it to make them smaller.

raw_text: Quick tech PSA because three people asked me this week: if you open a website and it still looks like the old version even though you know it's been changed, your browser is probably showing you a saved copy. Browsers keep pieces of sites you visit, like images, layouts, and scripts, so they don't have to download everything from scratch every time. That's called caching, and it's the reason your favorite sites load fast. The downside is that sometimes the browser holds onto those saved files a little too long and doesn't notice the site has been updated. A normal refresh asks it to check again, but it might still reuse some of what it saved. A "hard refresh" (Ctrl+Shift+R on Windows, Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac) tells it to skip the saved stuff and grab everything fresh. If that still doesn't work, clearing your browser's cache in settings usually does it. So no, you're not imagining it, and the site probably isn't broken. 🙂

raw_text: Fun thing I learned this week: your phone never actually talks to GPS satellites. It just listens. Each satellite constantly broadcasts a signal that basically says "this is exactly what time it is up here, and this is exactly where I am in orbit." Your phone picks up those broadcasts and notices that each one arrives a tiny fraction of a second late, because the signal had to travel thousands of miles to reach you. Multiply that delay by the speed of light and you get your distance from that satellite. With four or more of them overhead, your phone can work out the one spot on Earth that matches all those distances, and the extra satellite also helps it correct for its own clock not being anywhere near as precise as the atomic clocks on board. So the satellites have no idea you exist, and millions of people can use them at once without slowing anything down. (Your phone does sometimes grab a head start from cell towers or Wi-Fi to lock on faster, but the satellite part is all one-way.)

raw_text: Fun fact I learned this week and now can't stop telling people: "monsoon" doesn't actually mean rain. The word comes from the Arabic *mawsim*, meaning "season," and Arab sailors used it for the winds in the Indian Ocean that flip direction at roughly the same time every year. That flip is the whole idea. In summer, land heats up much faster than the ocean, so warm air rises over places like India and pulls in moist air off the sea, and all that moisture comes down as those famous downpours. In winter it runs the other way: the land cools off, and dry winds blow from the continent back out toward the ocean. So there's a "dry monsoon" too, which nobody ever talks about. The rain is really a side effect of the wind changing sides. Anyway, this is why my weather app calling a random thunderstorm "monsoon-like" now bothers me more than it should.

When the climate warmed and the ice melted roughly 10,000 to 20,000 years ago, all that meltwater raised sea levels around the world. The ocean simply poured into the deep valleys the glaciers had left behind. That's why you can be on a boat in seawater over a kilometer deep in Sognefjord while waterfalls come down cliffs on both sides. TOPIC:
Why do many places around the Mediterranean have relatively mild, wet winters and hot, dry summers? Write a concise post describing the broad climate pattern.
raw_text: Got back from Crete last week and kept wondering why the hills were brown and crispy in June when friends said it rained for weeks in January. So I looked it up. In summer, a big zone of high pressure that normally sits over the Atlantic near the Azores drifts north and parks itself over the Mediterranean. High pressure means air sinking from above, which warms and dries out as it comes down, so clouds barely form and you get those endless blue-sky days. In winter that high slides back south, and the storm systems that usually stay up over northern Europe can finally swing down across the sea, which is when most of the year's rain shows up. The sea itself keeps winters from getting very cold, because it holds onto summer heat and releases it slowly. That's why you see the same olive trees, vineyards, and dry scrub in places as far apart as southern Spain, Greece, and the coast of Lebanon. Turns out California, central Chile, and parts of South Africa and Australia have the same setup, which is why they're often called "Mediterranean climates" too.

raw_text: Had a friend ask me yesterday why her espresso and my pour-over tasted like totally different drinks when we'd bought the same bag of beans. The short answer is that it's all in how the water gets through the coffee. Espresso uses a very fine grind and a machine that forces hot water through it under a lot of pressure, so you get a shot in about 25-30 seconds. That pressure pulls out oils and solids fast, which is why a shot is thick, intense, and has that layer of tan foam (crema) on top. Filter coffee goes the slow way: a coarser grind, water just dripping through with gravity for 3-4 minutes, and usually a paper filter that catches most of the oils. You end up with something lighter and cleaner, where it's easier to pick out fruity or nutty flavors. Then there's how you drink it: espresso is an ounce or two in a tiny cup, or the base for a latte or cappuccino, while filter is a full mug you sip over half an hour. Fun fact that surprised her: that big mug of drip often has more total caffeine than a single shot, even though the shot tastes way stronger.

In yogurt, the same kind of acid makes milk proteins clump together, which is why it thickens instead of staying liquid. The acid also makes it hard for spoilage bugs to grow, which is how people kept vegetables and milk around long before refrigerators. Kind of wild that a tiny bacterium is behind three foods from opposite sides of the world.

raw_text: Started learning Japanese this month and finally figured out why every sentence looks like three different alphabets got mixed together. It's because they did. Kanji are the characters borrowed from Chinese, and they carry the "meat" of a sentence: nouns and the stems of verbs and adjectives, like 食 for "eat." Hiragana are the rounded characters that handle the grammar around those words, like verb endings, particles, and words that don't have a common kanji. Katakana, the sharper-looking set, are mostly for foreign loanwords (コーヒー is literally "kōhī," coffee), plus sound effects and emphasis. I kept wondering why they didn't just pick one, and it turns out Chinese characters were never a great fit for Japanese grammar, which changes word endings constantly, so the kana were developed from simplified kanji to fill that gap. But dropping kanji entirely would be rough too, because Japanese has a ton of words that sound identical, and written Japanese doesn't put spaces between words. The kanji make it clear which meaning is intended and show you where one word stops and the next begins, so the mix actually makes sense once you see each script doing its own job.

raw_text: My nephew is taking Spanish and asked me last night why a table is "a girl." Fair question! So "dialect" isn't wrong exactly, it just doesn't mean what most English speakers think it means.

English spreads that information across separate little words, while Turkish packs it into the word itself, and each suffix always shows up in the same order. There are hundreds of them around the world, because they grew out of Deaf communities the same way spoken languages grow out of hearing ones. That's why American Sign Language and British Sign Language are completely different, even though both countries speak English. Same thing with music: Beethoven's symphonies are public domain, but an orchestra's recording from 2015 belongs to whoever made that recording. You can perform the piece yourself, but you can't just rip their track and upload it as your own. raw_text: Went down a rabbit hole last night reading about film restoration, and it's way more than just "cleaning up" an old movie. A lot of the time there isn't even one complete copy left. Restorers end up piecing a film together from prints scattered across different archives and countries, some of them shortened or censored. When Metropolis was restored in 2010, about 25 minutes of lost footage came from a battered 16mm copy found in Buenos Aires, and it was so scratched that you can still tell exactly which scenes came from it. Then there's the stuff you'd never think about: color that has faded to pink over decades, nitrate film that's literally decaying, soundtracks full of crackle, and silent films that were originally tinted blue or amber, which someone has to reconstruct from old notes. And every fix is a judgment call. Scrub out too much grain or "correct" the color too hard and you've made something that looks nice but isn't what audiences saw in 1927. Honestly I'm going to watch the next restored classic with a lot more respect for the people who fought over every frame.

Since all the performers were men, that's also how female characters got played. The chorus wore matching masks, which made them look like one group (a crowd of elders, say) instead of fifteen random dudes. Some historians think the open mouth of the mask helped push the voice out a little, though that part is still argued about. Next time I see those smiling/frowning theatre masks on a poster I'm going to think about some poor actor sweating under linen and plaster in the Athenian sun.

raw_text: My sister told me yesterday she's never shaving her arms because "it'll just come back thicker," and I realized I believed that too until a few years ago. A hair that grows out on its own has a thin, tapered tip, but when you shave, you cut it straight across at the thicker part of the shaft. So the stubble that comes back has a blunt edge, and that's why it feels coarse and prickly when you run your hand over it. It can also look darker, partly because those short new hairs haven't had time to get lightened by sun and washing, and partly because dark stubble just stands out more against your skin. None of that changes the follicle under the skin, which decides how thick the hair is and how fast it grows, and a razor never gets anywhere near it. Researchers have actually tested this, going back as far as the 1920s, and shaved hair didn't come back any thicker or faster. So shave or don't, sis, but do it for your own reasons and not because of the myth 😄

Bats are not actually blind. Write a short post explaining what echolocation adds to their senses and why the phrase 'blind as a bat' is misleading.
raw_text: Had a bat swooping around our porch light last night, and my kid said "they can't see anything, right?" Turns out that's wrong. Every bat species has working eyes, and the big fruit bats (flying foxes) see quite well. Many of them don't echolocate at all and find fruit using sight and smell. The smaller insect-eating bats do use echolocation. They make high-pitched calls, mostly too high for us to hear, and listen to the echoes to figure out how far away a moth is, how big it is, and which way it's flying. That gives them a way to hunt in total darkness, but it works alongside their eyes rather than replacing them. So "blind as a bat" doesn't really hold up, since a bat in the dark is probably picking up more of what's around it than we would.

raw_text: Okay, tiny space pet peeve: there’s no permanent “dark side” of the Moon. The far side gets just as much sunlight as the side we see—it’s only “dark” in the sense that we can’t see it from Earth. We see nearly the same lunar face because the Moon is tidally locked: it takes about the same time to spin once on its axis as it does to orbit us. So as it circles Earth, it keeps the same hemisphere pointed our way. The far side isn’t stuck in eternal night; when we see a new moon, the far side is actually the one getting lit by the Sun. We do get to peek around the edges a bit thanks to a wobble called libration, so over time we see about 59% of the Moon’s surface. But that familiar face? That’s just the side that happens to be turned toward us.

raw_text: Every cold season I hear someone ask why antibiotics can’t just knock out a cold, so here’s the short version. Antibiotics are built to attack bacteria—things like their cell walls, their protein-making machinery, or how they copy their DNA. Viruses are a different kind of thing entirely: they’re basically a small bundle of genetic material wrapped in a protein shell. They can’t reproduce on their own, so they break into your cells and hijack your own machinery to make more copies of themselves. Antibiotics don’t have a good target in a virus, which is why they can’t stop it or cure the cold. That’s also why most colds, flu, and other viral infections don’t get better faster with antibiotics. Taking them anyway just risks side effects and helps create resistant bacteria. If a cold turns into a sinus or ear infection, a doctor might prescribe antibiotics—but that’s for a bacterial problem riding along, not the virus itself.

raw_text: I always thought jet lag was just the price of a long flight—like being extra tired. But it’s really your internal clock being out of sync with the local one. Your body runs on a circadian rhythm, a roughly 24-hour schedule that tells you when to sleep, wake, eat, and even when to feel alert. That clock takes its cues mostly from light, and it doesn’t reset instantly just because you got on a plane. So if you fly from New York to London, your body is still on New York time: at 11 p.m. London time, it thinks it’s 6 p.m., and you’re wide awake. Then at 7 a.m. London time, it’s convinced it’s the middle of the night, so you feel foggy and hungry at weird hours. That mismatch is why sleep at the destination can feel so wrong—you’re tired, but your body’s timing is still somewhere over the Atlantic.

That's why a 10 MB JPEG usually stays close to 10 MB inside a zip.

raw_text: I used to think falling prices were automatically a win. Cheaper groceries, cheaper rent, cheaper tech? Yes please. But economists worry about *sustained* deflation—when prices across the whole economy keep dropping year after year. If people expect things to be cheaper next month, many will delay buying, and that waiting can snowball: businesses sell less, cut hours or lay people off, and incomes fall, which makes everyone even more cautious. It also makes existing debt heavier, because the money you owe stays the same while your paycheck or business revenue shrinks. And central banks have a hard time fighting it, since they can’t cut interest rates much below zero. So the problem isn’t that cheaper goods are inherently bad—it’s that a broad, ongoing price drop can signal and feed a weak economy. A sale is great; a permanent, economy-wide markdown is a different story.

Its borders follow that geography too: Peru to the north, Bolivia and Argentina along the Andes to the east, and the Pacific to the west. It stretches over 4,300 km north to south but averages only about 177 km wide. Basically, Chile is long because the land between the ocean and the Andes is long, and narrow because there isn’t much room between them.

raw_text: Okay, climate nerd moment: why does the Mediterranean get rainy winters and bone-dry summers? In winter, the storm track and jet stream slide south, so low-pressure systems can march in off the Atlantic and Mediterranean and drop a lot of rain. In summer, the subtropical high—often the Azores High—bulges north and parks itself over the region. That high pushes air downward, which kills cloud formation and keeps rain away for weeks. The sea helps too: it keeps coastal winters from getting too cold and summers from being totally scorching right at the shore. So it’s basically a seasonal tug-of-war between mid-latitude storms and a dry subtropical high. Not every spot fits perfectly—mountains and islands have their own quirks—but that’s the broad pattern.

raw_text: I used to think film restoration just meant hitting "enhance" on an old movie. Turns out restorers spend most of their time dealing with missing chunks, torn frames, chemical damage, and soundtracks that have basically dissolved. They might have to piece a scene together from three different prints, borrow a reel from another archive, or decide whether to leave in a splice bump because removing it would mean cutting out a few frames of the only surviving take. Color is its own headache: faded dyes, tinted sequences, and prints that looked completely different depending on the lab or the country they were shown in. Then there's audio—crackle, hiss, missing dialogue—and the question of whether to clean it up until it sounds like a modern movie or keep some of the original texture. And every choice has a trade-off: do you make it look pristine, or do you preserve the evidence of how people actually saw it? Restorers aren't just sharpening a picture; they're rebuilding a thing that barely survived and guessing at what was lost. It's part detective work, part surgery, and part ethical debate.

The catch is that antibiotics only kill bacteria, not viruses. Bacteria are actual living, single-celled organisms, so antibiotics can target their cell walls or stop them from multiplying. Viruses, on the other hand, are basically just tiny packets of genetic code that hijack your own cells to reproduce. Because a virus hides inside your cells and doesn't have the same biological machinery as bacteria, the antibiotic has absolutely nothing to attack. The result is a standard mug of coffee that's lighter and less concentrated, meant to be sipped over time. Because it's not punching you in the face with intensity, a good filter brew actually makes it easier to taste the subtle, fruity, or earthy notes hiding in the bean.

raw_text: Fun fact: the Great Wall of China isn’t visible from the Moon with the naked eye. Even then, it can be harder to see than cities, highways, airports, dams, and large artificial islands. From the Moon, no individual human-made structure is visible without assistance. Swallowing one piece by accident is generally harmless, though swallowing large amounts—especially repeatedly—can rarely cause a blockage. So there’s no need to panic, but the trash can is still the better option.

TOPIC:
A popular claim says toilets always swirl in opposite directions in the northern and southern hemispheres. Write a short post explaining why household toilets are dominated by their design and initial water motion rather than the Coriolis effect.
raw_text: You’ve probably heard that toilets swirl one way in the Northern Hemisphere and the opposite way in the Southern Hemisphere. It’s a fun claim, but ordinary toilets don’t work that way. The direction of the swirl is mostly determined by the shape of the bowl, the placement of the water jets, and how the water starts moving. The Coriolis effect does influence huge systems like hurricanes, but it’s far too weak to control a quick toilet flush. In carefully controlled experiments with still water, its influence can sometimes be measured. For household toilets, though, the plumbing wins every time.
